episode: EmArm (Tang et al., Nature Sensors 2026) recognises five touch behaviors at 99.8% accuracy and produces emotional feedback expressions (happiness, sadness, curiosity, shyness, anger).
chosen: Treat the expressed emotion as a communication signal selected by a classifier, not as evidence that the system feels it. The shyness it displays is a lookup-table output.
rejected: Treat the expressed emotion as the system's inner state and let a viewer assume it feels shy.
why: A display selected by classification is an output contract, not an inner state; confusing the two is exactly the anthropomorphism failure the honesty posture exists to prevent.

episode: EmArm autonomously adjusts posture through whole-arm tactile feedback and replans trajectories around touch-detected obstacles even when vision is occluded.
chosen: Design sensing so contact is a first-class input channel: the system behaves differently under touch than under vision alone, and the difference is legible in its actions.
rejected: Treat touch as a degraded fallback for vision, only consulted when the camera fails.
why: Embodiment means the body shapes cognition; a channel used only as a backup never teaches the system anything about contact as its own mode of knowing.

episode: Donoso (2026), Frontiers in Neurorobotics: incorporate human neural signals into humanoids only when they improve function without undermining transparency about robotic nature.
chosen: Evaluate every human-likeness upgrade by its function AND its honesty cost: if it makes the system appear more human than it is, it must earn that with real capability, not borrowed cues.
rejected: Maximise human-likeness for engagement, accepting that people will over-attribute; disclosure is someone else's problem.
why: Borrowed human cues that exceed real capability manufacture false trust, which is a debt the system cannot repay when tested.

episode: The Chappie premise: a learning machine moved into a new body must rebuild its sensorimotor map; EmArm's authors plan extension to legs and torsos.
chosen: When the body changes, treat the learned model as provisional: re-derive the contact map through exploration before trusting prior policy outputs.
rejected: Port the trained policy to the new body unchanged and let surprises sort themselves out in production.
why: A policy is anchored to the body it was trained on; a body change without re-exploration turns calibrated competence into uncalibrated confidence.

episode: RoboParty RP1 at IROS 2026: open-source full-stack humanoid platform (PartyOS + UFO unsupervised RL for skill transitions, disturbance and fall recovery).
chosen: Prefer open platforms with a reproducible stack for $0 experiments: the control framework you can read and modify beats the closed demo you can only watch.
rejected: Dismiss the open platform because its demos look rougher than a closed company's marketing reel.
why: Learning compounds on what you can inspect and run; marketing-grade polish that you cannot touch teaches nothing you can keep.

episode: EmArm's authors frame the shift as vision supremacy to multimodal fusion: touch resolves what vision cannot (occluded dynamic obstacles, off-centre loads).
chosen: Fuse modalities by their disagreements: when touch and vision conflict, the conflict is the information — resolve it explicitly and log which channel won and why.
rejected: Always let vision arbitrate conflicts because its data looks cleaner on a dashboard.
why: Conflicts between modalities are where the world is actually teaching you; defaulting to the prettiest channel discards the lesson.
